questions.question: What are derived query methods in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: Derived Query Methods in Spring Data JPA — Name-Based Query Generation
questions.direct_answer: **Derived query methods** let Spring Data JPA generate the query from the **method name**. Declaring `findByLastName(String name)` produces `WHERE last_name = ?` — no SQL, no `@Query`. Spring **parses the name at startup** into a query, so a typo or unknown field fails the application boot (fast feedback), not at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand name-based query generation and that names are validated at startup against entity fields
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing @Query JPQL for simple conditions derived methods already handle, or omitting @Transactional on deleteBy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention startup-time parsing/validation and the keyword grammar (And, Or, GreaterThan, Between, OrderBy, Top)

sections.title: Auto-Generated Queries from Method Names
sections.content:
**Derived query methods** are Spring Data JPA's headline productivity feature: you declare a method signature in a repository interface following a naming grammar, and Spring generates the query implementation **at application startup** — no `@Query`, no SQL, no implementation class.

Spring reads `findByLastNameAndAge(String lastName, int age)` and turns it into `WHERE last_name = ? AND age = ?`. Each keyword maps to a SQL fragment: `findBy` → SELECT, `And`/`Or` → boolean logic, `Between`/`GreaterThan`/`In` → operators, `OrderBy` → sorting. If the name breaks the grammar or references an unknown field, the app **fails fast at boot** with a `PropertyReferenceException` — a clear, early error instead of a production surprise.

sections.title: Derived Method Grammar at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Subject keyword|~What it does|findBy / getBy / readBy = SELECT|countBy = COUNT|existsBy = EXISTS, deleteBy = DELETE
blue|Conditions|~The WHERE clause|And / Or|GreaterThan, LessThan, Between, In|IsNull, Containing
emerald|Modifiers|~Shape the result|OrderBy...Asc/Desc|Top / First N|IgnoreCase, Distinct
violet|Validation|~Fail fast|parsed at startup|fields matched to entity|typo = boot error, not runtime

sections.title: A Repository Full of Derived Methods
sections.content:
```java
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {

    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);                 // WHERE last_name = ?

    Optional<User> findByEmailAndStatus(String email, String status); // AND

    List<User> findByAgeGreaterThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc(int age);     // > ? ORDER BY ... DESC

    List<User> findByCreatedAtBetween(LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end); // BETWEEN

    long countByDepartment(String department);                 // COUNT(*)

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);                        // EXISTS

    @Transactional
    void deleteByStatus(String status);                        // DELETE — needs a transaction
}
```

sections.title: Wrong — Misspelled Property in the Method Name
Right — Property Names Match the Entity Fields
sections.content:
```java
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    List<User> findByLastName(String lastName);   // matches User.lastName
    List<User> findByEmail(String email);         // matches User.email
}
```
Spring validates every property against the entity at startup, so a typo fails the boot, not production.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Field-name typos** — `findByNameLastName` instead of `findByLastName`; the property must match the entity field, else `PropertyReferenceException` at startup.
- **`deleteBy` without `@Transactional`** — throws `TransactionRequiredException` at runtime; writes need a transaction.
- **Overusing derived methods** — `findByFirstNameAndLastNameAndAgeAndDepartmentAndStatus` is unreadable; switch to `@Query` past ~3 conditions.
- **Reaching for `@Query` too early** — for simple `findByEmail`, a derived method is cleaner.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Method name → query** — Spring parses it at **startup** and generates the implementation.
- **Subject keywords**: `findBy`, `countBy`, `existsBy`, `deleteBy`.
- **Conditions/operators**: `And`, `Or`, `GreaterThan`, `Between`, `In`, `IsNull`, `Containing`.
- **Result shaping**: `OrderBy...Asc/Desc`, `Top`/`First`, `IgnoreCase`, `Distinct`.
- **`deleteBy` needs `@Transactional`**; typos fail at boot, not at runtime.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Derived query methods are a Spring Data JPA feature where I just write a method signature in my repository interface and Spring generates the query by reading the method name. For example, if I write findByLastName with a String parameter, Spring builds a select with a where clause on the last name field. I don't write any SQL or annotations. This works because Spring parses the method name at application startup. It breaks the name into parts — findBy means it's a select, LastName maps to the last name field on my entity, and the parameter becomes a where condition. I can combine conditions with And or Or, like findByEmailAndStatus. There are operator keywords too, like findByAgeGreaterThan, and result shapers like OrderBy, Top, and IgnoreCase. The mistake freshers make is writing a custom Query annotation for simple lookups that a derived method handles perfectly. Another gotcha is delete methods: if I write deleteByStatus I have to add Transactional, or it throws at runtime. Something interviewers like to hear is that if my method name doesn't follow the grammar or references a field that doesn't exist, the application fails at startup with a clear error, which is much better than discovering it in production. So derived methods keep repositories clean and readable, and when the names get long with many conditions, that's the signal to switch to a Query annotation with JPQL.

questions.question: What is the findBy...Containing and findBy...Like in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: Containing, Like, StartingWith — String Matching in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: **`Containing`** → `LIKE '%text%'` (Spring adds both wildcards). **`StartingWith`** → `LIKE 'text%'`, **`EndingWith`** → `LIKE '%text'`. **`Like`** passes your pattern as-is — **you** add the `%`. Append **`IgnoreCase`** for case-insensitive search. Note: a **leading `%` can't use an index**, so `StartingWith` is faster than `Containing` on big tables.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which keywords add wildcards automatically and the index/performance impact of a leading %
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Passing %text% to Containing (double wildcards) or omitting % with Like and getting an exact match
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention IgnoreCase for user search and that leading % forces a full scan (StartingWith is index-friendly)

sections.title: String Pattern Matching in Derived Queries
sections.content:
Spring Data offers several keywords for `LIKE` matching. **`Containing`**, **`StartingWith`**, and **`EndingWith`** add the `%` wildcards **for you**; **`Like`** expects the **full pattern including wildcards**.

`findByNameContaining("john")` → `WHERE name LIKE '%john%'`. `findByNameLike("john%")` → `WHERE name LIKE 'john%'` exactly. Append **`IgnoreCase`** for case-insensitive search (`LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER(...)`). **Performance**: a leading wildcard (`%text`) can't use an index, so `Containing`/`EndingWith` force a full scan on large tables, while `StartingWith` (`text%`) stays index-friendly.

sections.title: String Matchers at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Containing|~Both wildcards auto|LIKE %text%|pass raw text|general search box
blue|StartingWith|~Trailing wildcard|LIKE text%|index-friendly|autocomplete / prefixes
emerald|EndingWith|~Leading wildcard|LIKE %text|full scan risk|suffix / domain match
violet|Like|~You add wildcards|pattern as-is|_ matches one char|full control
rose|IgnoreCase|~Case-insensitive|LOWER() both sides|append to any matcher|user-facing search

sections.title: Wrong — Double Wildcards and Missing Wildcards
Right — Let Containing Add Wildcards; Add Them Yourself for Like
sections.content:
```java
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    List<Product> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String keyword); // pass raw "phone"
    List<Product> findByNameStartingWith(String prefix);          // "Apple" → 'Apple%'
    List<Product> findByNameLike(String pattern);                 // you pass "%phone%"
}

// usage
repo.findByNameContainingIgnoreCase("phone"); // LOWER(name) LIKE LOWER('%phone%')
repo.findByNameLike("%phone%");               // you supply the wildcards
```
For user-facing search always use `IgnoreCase`; prefer `StartingWith` on large tables for index use.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding `%` to `Containing`** — `findByNameContaining("%phone%")` becomes `LIKE '%%phone%%'`; pass raw text.
- **Forgetting `%` with `Like`** — `findByNameLike("john")` is an exact match; you must pass `%john%`.
- **Skipping `IgnoreCase`** — "iPhone" won't match "iphone"; users expect case-insensitive search.
- **Ignoring performance** — `Containing` on a 10M-row table does a full scan because the leading `%` defeats indexes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Containing`/`StartingWith`/`EndingWith` add `%` for you**; pass raw text.
- **`Like` needs your own wildcards** (`%`, and `_` for a single char).
- **`IgnoreCase`** makes search case-insensitive via `LOWER()`.
- **Leading `%` can't use an index** — `StartingWith` is fastest; `Containing` scans.
- **Empty string to `Containing`** matches everything — validate input.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Spring Data has keywords for string matching in method names. The main ones are Containing, StartingWith, EndingWith, and Like. Containing is the most common — findByNameContaining with the string phone generates a like with percent phone percent. It adds the wildcards on both sides for me. StartingWith adds the wildcard only at the end, so prefix percent, and EndingWith puts it at the start. The key difference is Like, which doesn't add any wildcards. I have to provide the full pattern myself, so findByNameLike with just john is an exact match — I'd need percent john percent for a search. A really important one is the IgnoreCase suffix. findByNameContainingIgnoreCase makes the search case-insensitive by lowercasing both sides, which matters for user searches because people don't care about case. The mistake freshers make is adding wildcards when using Containing — they pass percent phone percent, which gives double wildcards and breaks the query. The other big topic is performance. With Containing or EndingWith, the leading percent means the database can't use an index, so on a big table it scans every row. StartingWith is faster because prefix percent can use an index, which is why autocomplete uses StartingWith. If someone needs more control, like matching a single character with an underscore, that's when Like is the right choice.

questions.question: How do you use findBy...In() and findBy...Between() in Spring Data?
questions.title: findByIn and findByBetween in Spring Data JPA — Collection and Range Queries
questions.direct_answer: **`findByStatusIn(Collection)`** → `WHERE status IN (...)`. **`findByAgeBetween(min, max)`** → `WHERE age BETWEEN min AND max` (inclusive both ends). `findByIdIn(List<Long>)` is the standard bulk-fetch pattern. Watch out: an **empty collection** with `In` makes invalid SQL, and some databases cap `IN` size (e.g. Oracle 1000).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you reach for In/Between instead of custom @Query for multi-value and range filters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing In exists (writing @Query for IN), or passing an empty list and breaking the SQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention findByIdIn for bulk fetch, BETWEEN being inclusive, and IN-clause size limits

sections.title: Collection and Range Queries
sections.content:
**`In`** and **`Between`** filter by collections or ranges without custom SQL. **`findBy<Property>In(Collection)`** generates `WHERE property IN (...)` — ideal for multiple allowed values (statuses, category IDs). **`findBy<Property>Between(start, end)`** generates `WHERE property BETWEEN start AND end`, inclusive on **both** ends, working with numbers, dates, and any `Comparable`.

These cover most multi-value/range filtering in REST APIs: products by category list, users by age range, orders by date range. Caveat: very large `IN` collections can hit database limits — batch them if needed.

sections.title: In and Between at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|In|~Multiple values|WHERE status IN (...)|works with List/Set|findByIdIn = bulk fetch
blue|Between|~A range|WHERE age BETWEEN a AND b|inclusive both ends|numbers, dates, Comparable
emerald|Exclusive range|~Need open bounds|GreaterThan + LessThan|combine with And|when BETWEEN won't do
violet|Limits|~Watch out|empty list = invalid SQL|Oracle caps IN at 1000|batch large lists

sections.title: Wrong — Custom @Query for IN, and an Unguarded Empty List
Right — Derived In/Between with an Empty-List Guard
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing `In` exists** — writing a custom `@Query` IN clause when `findByStatusIn` does it.
- **Empty collection** — `findByStatusIn(List.of())` → `IN ()`, invalid SQL; guard or validate.
- **Wrong `Between` boundaries** — `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` includes both 10 and 20; use `GreaterThan`/`LessThan` for exclusive ranges.
- **Timezone bugs** — using `LocalDateTime.now()` in date ranges without timezone care causes off-by-hours errors.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`findByPropertyIn(Collection)`** → `IN (...)`; works with `List`/`Set`.
- **`findByPropertyBetween(a, b)`** is **inclusive** on both ends.
- **`findByIdIn(List<Long>)`** is the standard bulk-fetch-by-ids pattern.
- **Empty collections break `In`** — validate before calling.
- **`IN` size limits** exist (e.g. Oracle 1000) — batch very large lists.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: In and Between are derived-query keywords for filtering by multiple values or by a range. If I write findByStatusIn and pass a list like pending, processing, shipped, Spring generates a where status in clause with those values. This is very common in REST APIs — for example filtering orders by a multi-select of statuses, or the really common findByIdIn pattern where I pass a list of ids and get them all back in one query, which beats looping and calling findById repeatedly. Between is for ranges. findByAgeBetween with two parameters generates where age between the min and max, and it works with numbers, dates, any comparable type. A typical use case is a date range, like orders created in the last seven days, or a price filter on an e-commerce site. One thing to remember is that between is inclusive on both ends, so between ten and twenty includes ten and twenty. If I need an exclusive range I'd use GreaterThan and LessThan combined with And. The mistake freshers make is not knowing In exists, so they write a custom query with an IN clause. Another gotcha is passing an empty list to a method with In — that produces where status in with nothing, which is invalid SQL, so I guard the empty case before calling. And in interviews it stands out to mention findByIdIn as a bulk-fetch pattern and to note that some databases cap the IN size — Oracle around a thousand — so for very large lists I'd batch the queries.

followup_questions: How do you fetch multiple entities by a list of IDs efficiently?
What is the difference Between and GreaterThanEqual/LessThanEqual?

questions.question: How do you limit query results with Top and First in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: findTop and findFirst in Spring Data JPA — Limiting Query Results
questions.direct_answer: Put **`Top`** or **`First`** in the method name to limit rows via a SQL **`LIMIT`**. `findTop3ByOrderByCreatedAtDesc()` fetches the 3 newest; `findFirstByStatus(...)` returns one (`findFirst` = `findTop1`). Always pair with **`OrderBy`** — without it you get arbitrary rows. This limits at the **database**, not by loading all rows then trimming in Java.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you limit at the database level and know Top/First are synonyms requiring OrderBy to be meaningful
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling findAll() then Stream.limit() — loads everything into memory instead of using SQL LIMIT
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note findFirst equals findTop1, and combining Top with OrderBy gives efficient 'latest N' queries

sections.title: Result Limiting with Top and First
sections.content:
**`Top`** and **`First`** limit results right in the method name, generating a SQL **`LIMIT`** so the database returns only the rows you need — far cheaper than fetching all and trimming in Java. **`findFirst`** and **`findTop1`** are synonyms (one row); use any count: `findTop5`, `findTop10`.

The power is combining them with **`OrderBy`**: `findTop3ByOrderByTotalDesc()` gives the 3 highest totals. Without ordering you get arbitrary rows (insertion order), which is rarely useful — perfect for dashboards, recent-activity feeds, and leaderboards.

sections.title: Top / First at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|findFirst / findTop1|~Single row|returns Optional<T>|same thing|most-recent / highest
blue|findTopN|~N rows|returns List<T>|SQL LIMIT N|top 5, top 10, ...
emerald|+ OrderBy|~Makes it meaningful|...OrderByCreatedAtDesc|latest / oldest / highest|required for sense
violet|vs Stream.limit|~Where it happens|LIMIT at the DB|not load-all-then-trim|memory + speed win

sections.title: Wrong — Load Everything, Limit in Java
sections.content:
```java
// Loads ALL matching rows into memory, then throws most away
List<Order> recent = orderRepository.findAll().stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::getCreatedAt).reversed())
        .limit(5)
        .toList();
```

sections.title: Right — LIMIT at the Database with Top/First
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`findAll()` + `Stream.limit()`** — loads thousands of rows to keep 5; use `Top`/`First`.
- **Forgetting `OrderBy`** — `findTop10ByStatus(...)` returns 10 arbitrary rows, not the 10 you want.
- **Confusing First and Top** — both limit; `findFirst` = `findTop1`, just naming style.
- **Expecting null** — `findTopN` returns a `List` (possibly empty); `findFirst` returns `Optional`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Top`/`First` generate SQL `LIMIT`** — limiting happens at the database.
- **`findFirst` = `findTop1`** — single row, returns `Optional`.
- **Pair with `OrderBy`** — otherwise rows are arbitrary.
- **Any count** — `findTop3`, `findTop10`, etc.
- **No `@Query` needed** — fully derived, optimized queries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Spring Data lets me limit results right in the method name using Top or First. If I write findTop3ByOrderByCreatedAtDesc, it generates SQL with a limit clause to fetch only the three most recent records. First and Top are the same thing — findFirst is just findTop1 with a friendlier name. The key is combining them with OrderBy, because without sorting I get arbitrary rows based on insertion order, which isn't useful. So for a dashboard that shows the latest five orders, I write findTop5ByOrderByCreatedAtDesc. This is much more efficient than calling findAll and then using a Java stream to limit, because that loads every order into memory first and throws most of them away. One detail freshers miss is that the return types differ — findFirst returns an Optional because it's a single record, while findTop5 returns a List. I can use any number, like Top10 or Top20. It's perfect for leaderboards, recent-activity feeds, and anywhere I need a small, sorted slice of data without writing a custom query.

followup_questions: What is the difference between findTop and findFirst in Spring Data JPA?
When would you use Pageable instead of findTop for limiting results?

questions.question: How do you write a custom JPQL query with @Query in Spring Data JPA?
questions.title: @Query Annotation in Spring Data JPA — JPQL and Native SQL
questions.direct_answer: Annotate a repository method with **`@Query`** and supply **JPQL** (entity/field names) — add **`nativeQuery = true`** for raw SQL. Bind values with **named** (`:param` + `@Param`) or positional (`?1`) parameters; named is clearer. For UPDATE/DELETE you must add **`@Modifying`** and run inside **`@Transactional`**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write JPQL/native queries and know the @Modifying + @Transactional requirement for writes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @Modifying/@Transactional on UPDATE/DELETE, or using table names in JPQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show JOIN FETCH for N+1, named vs positional params, and when nativeQuery=true is justified

sections.title: Custom Queries When Derived Methods Aren't Enough
sections.content:
**`@Query`** lets you write custom **JPQL** or **native SQL** when method names get unwieldy or you need joins, subqueries, or DB functions. JPQL uses **entity class and field names** (`FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email`), not table/column names. Add **`nativeQuery = true`** for raw SQL.

Bind values with **named** parameters (`:email` + `@Param`) — clearer and refactor-safe — or positional (`?1`). For **UPDATE/DELETE** you must add **`@Modifying`** and run within **`@Transactional`**, or Hibernate throws.

sections.title: @Query Options at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JPQL|~Entity-level|FROM User u (class)|u.email (field)|portable, validated
blue|Native|~nativeQuery = true|raw table SQL|DB functions (INTERVAL)|not portable
emerald|Params|~Binding|:name + @Param (named)|?1 (positional)|named preferred
violet|Writes|~UPDATE/DELETE|need @Modifying|need @Transactional|else exception
cyan|JOIN FETCH|~N+1 fix|load relation in one query|avoid lazy loops|performance

sections.title: Wrong — UPDATE Without @Modifying / Table Name in JPQL
Right — JPQL, JOIN FETCH, and a Proper @Modifying Update
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Missing `@Modifying`** on UPDATE/DELETE — Hibernate assumes a read query and throws.
- **No `@Transactional`** — even with `@Modifying`, writes need a transaction.
- **Table names in JPQL** — `FROM orders` fails; use the entity `FROM Order`.
- **Native query and entity state** — native results aren't managed; changes won't auto-flush unless you `save()`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JPQL uses entity/field names**; native SQL (`nativeQuery = true`) uses table/column names.
- **Named params** (`:p` + `@Param`) are clearer than positional `?1`.
- **`JOIN FETCH`** loads associations in one query, fixing N+1.
- **UPDATE/DELETE need `@Modifying`** and a `@Transactional` boundary.
- **Native results aren't managed entities** — be careful with updates.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: When derived query methods get too complex or I need a join, I use the Query annotation to write a custom query. I annotate the repository method and provide a JPQL string. JPQL is like SQL but uses entity class and field names instead of table and column names — so I write from Order o where o dot status equals something, not from orders. I bind values with named parameters using a colon, like colon status, and the Param annotation, which is more readable than positional parameters like question mark one. If I need database-specific SQL, I add native query equals true and write raw SQL. The big gotcha is update and delete queries. If I write an update with the Query annotation, I must also add the Modifying annotation, otherwise Hibernate throws because it expects a read query by default. And that method needs a transactional boundary, usually Transactional on the service. Another common use is JOIN FETCH to avoid the N plus one problem — if I'm loading orders and need their customers, join fetch o dot customer loads everything in one query instead of one query per order. Interviewers like to hear about named versus positional parameters and when I'd use native query — usually for performance tuning or PostgreSQL features like INTERVAL that JPQL doesn't have. One more thing worth noting is that JPQL queries can be validated at startup, so a syntax error is caught early rather than in production.

questions.question: When should you use @Query instead of a derived query method?
questions.title: @Query vs Derived Methods — Choosing the Right Approach
questions.direct_answer: Use **derived methods** for simple conditions (1-3 fields) where the name stays readable. Switch to **`@Query`** when the name exceeds ~60-70 chars, or you need **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG), subqueries, or DB-specific SQL** — things derived methods simply can't express. Readability and capability are the deciding factors.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment on the readability/capability trade-off between derived methods and @Query
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Cramming 5-6 conditions into a derived method name instead of a clear @Query, or thinking derived methods can do JOIN/GROUP BY

sections.title: Choosing Between Derived Methods and @Query
sections.content:
Spring Data offers two query styles: **derived methods** (the name defines the query) and **`@Query`** (you write JPQL/SQL). Derived methods are great for simple, self-documenting lookups — `findByEmail`, `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter`.

They break down as complexity grows. `findByStatusAndCategoryAndPriceGreaterThanAndCreatedAtBetweenOrderByPriceDesc` is unreadable and fragile. The decision rests on **readability** (past ~3 conditions or ~60-70 chars, prefer `@Query`) and **capability** — derived methods can't do JOINs, `GROUP BY`, aggregates, or subqueries, so those force `@Query`.

sections.title: Pick the Right Tool at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Derived method|~Simple lookups|1-3 conditions|self-documenting|no SQL needed
blue|@Query (JPQL)|~Complex but portable|joins, aggregates|named params|when names get long
emerald|@Query (native)|~DB-specific|JSONB, window fns|nativeQuery = true|last resort
violet|Readability rule|~The threshold|~60-70 char name|>3 conditions|switch to @Query

sections.title: Derived Methods vs @Query
sections.content:
| Need | Derived method | @Query |
|---|---|---|
| 1-3 simple conditions | Best fit | Overkill |
| 4+ conditions / long name | Unreadable | Best fit |
| JOIN across entities | Not possible | Required |
| GROUP BY / COUNT / SUM | Not possible | Required |
| Subqueries | Not possible | Required |
| DB-specific SQL | Not possible | `nativeQuery = true` |

Rule: more than a `WHERE` with AND/OR → use `@Query`.

sections.title: Wrong — A Six-Condition Derived Method Name
Right — Clear @Query (and an Aggregate Derived Methods Can't Do)
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **derived methods** for simple, readable lookups (1-3 conditions): `findByEmail`, `findByStatus`. Use **`@Query` with JPQL** when the name would balloon, when you need `JOIN`/`JOIN FETCH`, projections/DTOs, or aggregates like `COUNT`/`AVG`/`GROUP BY`. Use **`@Query(nativeQuery = true)`** for DB-specific features (PostgreSQL JSONB, full-text search) or heavy reporting SQL. The honest test: if you can't read the query at a glance, rewrite it as `@Query`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **1-3 conditions** → derived method; **4+ / long name** → `@Query`.
- **~60-70 char** method names are a readability red flag.
- **JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregates, subqueries** are impossible with derived methods.
- **Named `@Query` params** beat long positional derived parameter lists.
- **Native SQL** for DB-specific features via `nativeQuery = true`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I use derived query methods for simple lookups with one to three conditions where the method name stays readable. Something like findByEmailAndStatus is clear and self-documenting and needs no SQL. But once I'm adding a fourth or fifth condition, the name becomes a paragraph, and that's when I switch to the Query annotation. My rule of thumb is that if the method name is approaching sixty or seventy characters, it's time for JPQL. There are also hard technical limits — derived methods can't do joins, group by, or aggregate functions like count, sum, or average. If I need to join orders and customers, or compute the average order value per customer, I have to use the Query annotation because there's simply no derived syntax for it. The other reason is readability in complex cases: a short, clear JPQL query with named parameters is much easier to maintain than a giant method name with six parameters in a fixed order. A mistake I see freshers make is forcing a derived method for a complex query and ending up with something nobody can read. If I'm struggling to write the name or I'd have to document separately what it does, I just use the Query annotation. It's not more advanced, it's just the right tool for that job.
